coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: churn diagnosis, then pricing power by segment, then value of the rise, then SMB handling and roll-out. X is tighter, and every executive-summary line maps to a section with its supporting figures. Y sets out five key questions, answers each with a section summary of three findings tied to sub-slides, and bridges to the recommendation with an options table. Neither contradicts itself: both say the churn rise is not a list-price reaction yet hold SMB because of Inkwell, and both explain why. X compares a 7% enterprise break-even to the 2023 SMB response, which is slightly loose; Y's longer structure has some repetition. The difference is negligible.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the same defensible answer (R1/R2): 10% on mid-market, 7–10% on enterprise within caps, SMB held pending an 8% test, plus activation of the promotion cohort. Y weighs the alternatives better. It scores three options, including 'no rise' (which would need $4.9M of new-customer ARR), and names the branches it left out, such as a low-price SMB plan to revisit if the test fails. Y also treats the mid-market move as a risk to manage: it flags the unexplained 0.6% to 0.8% churn rise and holds part of Q1 renewals at today's price as a control, because the 2024 test covered new sign-ups only. Its triggers are concrete: 0.5 pp above control for SMB, first Inkwell sighting above 200 seats, and stopping activation spend if nothing moves. X's guardrail is weaker: 'pause any rise whose losses approach break-even' would tolerate about 9% extra loss in mid-market before acting. X has no mid-market control group and does not consider the no-rise option.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: promotion-cohort churn of about 4.9%, non-promotion SMB at 2.0% to 2.1%, the $7.6M reachable uplift, 3.6% extra loss in 2023, the rebuilt dashboard figures (1.7% to 2.6% and 0.8% to 1.2%), and the one-third (not one-half) ceiling on the onboarding claim. X's break-even rule p/(1+p) is clean and needs no assumptions. Y goes further on the critical evidence. It decomposes the whole churn rise (90.4% from the promotion cohort, with other SMB and mid-market shown separately). It nets the CFO's figure down to $6.3M after an SMB churn response, and its 1.98x break-even is equivalent to the key's 10.7%. It notes the 2024 test predates Inkwell and has no sample size, and that mid-market churn has risen for unknown reasons. Y's 12/8 scaling of the 2023 response is an assumption, but it is flagged and shown across a sensitivity table. X's headline 'even the smallest rise pays unless it loses nearly twice 2023's customers' applies an SMB precedent to enterprise and mid-market, a weaker inference. I found no material numerical errors in either.

revision.reasons: Both revise the CFO's hypothesis appropriately rather than adopting or rejecting it wholesale. Each accepts that the churn rise is mostly a promotion-cohort mix effect, which supports the CFO. Each rejects the uniform 12% and the $10.3M, and each keeps the CEO's concern alive for SMB through Inkwell and a gated test. X states the reconciliation most explicitly ('both views hold for this cohort: it needs onboarding, and it is the one group that reacts to price'). Y makes the same point through 'promotion churners blame price because their discount ended' and 'Inkwell has made new SMB buyers more price-sensitive, though existing customers have not yet moved', and further discounts the CFO's figure for churn. Both also cut the Customer Success 'halve churn' claim to about a third. The handling is equivalent in quality.

overall.reasons: The recommendations are essentially identical and both meet every defensibility criterion: mix effect separated from rate effect, both views reconciled, $10.3M corrected, pricing differentiated by segment. Y serves the CEO better on the points where the decision could go wrong. It tests the mid-market rise with a renewal control group instead of leaning on a new-sign-up test, and it flags the unexplained mid-market churn rise. It quantifies the SMB downside across response scenarios, compares against a no-rise option, and gives specific triggers and owners. X is more concise, has an elegant break-even treatment and states the reconciliation of the two views more explicitly. But its guardrails are looser and it treats mid-market pricing power as more settled than the evidence warrants.
